title: Leave Your Country, Your Relatives, Your Father's House — Leaving, Promise, Down to Egypt
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Last lesson left us in Haran. A family had set out for Canaan, settled down halfway there, and stayed settled until the father died. And the camera of Scripture has been narrowing all this time — from the seventy nations of the whole human race down to one household, one tent, one woman with no children.
In today's lesson God is going to open his mouth and speak to one man inside that household. And the first thing he says to him is a very hard thing to ask.

So let me put a question to you first. If God told you today to leave everything you know best, what would you ask? Most people would ask: Where to? For how long? Is it secure? What about the children?

Let me put the answer up front. God's call very often asks a person to set out first, and only then gives him the address. And what he asks a person to leave is never asked in order to take something away from him — it is so that all the families of the earth may be blessed through him.
Verse 1: "Now Yahweh said to Abram, 'Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father's house, and go to the land that I will show you.'"
"Leave" is two words in Hebrew: לֶךְ־לְךָ (*lech-lecha*). The first word means "go"; the second means "for yourself." So a literal rendering would be: "You go — go for yourself."

Brothers and sisters, that phrase occurs only twice in the whole Bible. Once here, and once in 22:2 — "Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah." The very same phrase. Twice in Abraham's lifetime God said to him, "Go": the first time it meant leave your past, and the second time it meant hand over your future.

Then notice the three layers: your country, your relatives, your father's house. They run from the widest down to the narrowest. "Your country" is land — it is where your sense of safety comes from. "Your relatives" is your people — it is your identity. "Your father's house", וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ (*umibeit avicha*), is the innermost ring of all — it is relationship, it is your backing, it is the first person you telephone when something goes wrong.
Brothers and sisters, God peels the layers off one at a time, until nothing is left but his word.

And the hardest line of all comes at the end: "go to the land that I will show you." Notice the tense — "that I will show you" — he has not shown it yet. God tells him to set out first and gives him the address afterwards. Hebrews 11:8 catches it beautifully: "He went out, not knowing where he went."
God told Abram to "leave your country, and your relatives, and your father's house." Does that mean everybody who comes to faith today ought to leave home too?

We have to be clear about the shape of a call. Abram's leaving was specific, it carried a promise, and it had a destination — God said, "go to the land that I will show you." The New Testament never turns "leave home" into a general command. Quite the opposite: the Lord Jesus sent the man who had been demon-possessed straight back home — "Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you." So the healthy way to discern this is: sometimes God tells a person to leave, and sometimes God tells a person to stay, and both of those are obedience. What every believer without exception does have to leave is the old reliances that keep us from following the Lord — that may be an over-dependence inside one relationship, and it may be a whole set of family values.
The original behind "go" is "go for yourself." Is that saying obedience is good for me?

The Hebrew לֶךְ־לְךָ (*lech lecha*) is literally "you go, for yourself", and the expression turns up only twice in the Bible — here in chapter 12, and in chapter 22, "go into the land of Moriah." Both times Abraham is being asked to hand over the thing he treasures most. So this "for yourself" is not a guarantee of a return on the transaction. It is saying that the one who is finally completed by this is you — you yourself, as a person. Obedience is not God taking something off you; it is God making something of you. And of course God does give promises in the very same speech — he never sends anybody out empty-handed. But the heart of those promises is not property. It is "You will be a blessing."
In verses 2 and 3 God gives seven promises, one after another:

"I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you."

The first thing: "I will make of you a great nation", גּוֹי גָּדוֹל (*goy gadol*). Brothers and sisters, that word גּוֹי is precisely the word used back in chapter 10 when the nations were being counted off. God intends to make another whole nation out of one man. And at this moment he is seventy-five years old, and he has no son.

The second thing: "make your name great", וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ (*va'agadlah shemecha*). Brothers and sisters, this is the direct, positive answer to the previous chapter. In 11:4 the people said, "let's make a name for ourselves", and they were scattered. In 12:2 God says, "I will bless you and make your name great." The same thing exactly — except that one lot grabbed at it and the other was handed it. That standing you are fighting for at this moment: which of the two is it?

The third thing, and the one most easily missed: "You will be a blessing", וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה (*vehyeh berachah*), which is literally "be a blessing." Not "you will get blessed" — "be a blessing." It is as much a commission as it is a gift. Brothers and sisters, everything God gives you has a "for whose sake" on the far end of it.

The fourth thing — the wording of verse 3 is very interesting. "Those who bless you" is plural; "him who treats you with contempt" is singular. The ones who bless are a crowd; the one who curses is only one. And "I will curse" uses the word אָאֹר (*a'or*), from the root אָרַר — the heavier of the two Hebrew words for cursing, the one God used in 3:14 when he cursed the serpent.

The fifth thing, and the purpose of the whole passage: "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you." "All the families", כֹּל מִשְׁפְּחֹת הָאֲדָמָה, is exactly the word used of those seventy families that chapter 10 counted out.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the structure? Chapter 10: seventy families. Chapter 11: scattered. Chapter 12: one man chosen, in order to bless those seventy families. Galatians 3:8 says, "The Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Good News beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you all the nations will be blessed.'" Paul is telling us that this verse is the gospel.
The threefold promise has land in it, and a nation, and blessing. Has any of that anything to do with Christians today?

It has, and the New Testament picks it up directly. Galatians 3 says the promise was "that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Christ Jesus", and it says, "If you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise." So the third strand — "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you" — is being fulfilled in you and in me right now. What we have to watch is the privatising of the promise. Every single blessing God gives Abram has somebody else at the end of the sentence — "You will be a blessing." So a faith that assumes being blessed simply means having a comfortable life of one's own has read this chapter exactly backwards.
"Be a blessing" sounds lovely, but I can barely keep my own head above water. What have I got to give?

Start by getting the definition of "blessing" right. The blessing in this chapter is not wealth; it is God's presence and God's promise reaching a person. So what you have to give is usually not something you have to spare — it is the One you are going through this with. A person in the middle of hardship, if he is willing to say one true sentence to another person in hardship and to sit with him for half an hour, has given a blessing. And notice the order of the text: God says "I will bless you" first, and only then "You will be a blessing." You are not squeezing something out of yourself; you are receiving first. A practical suggestion: this week do one small thing — the thing you can actually manage at this moment — and do not wait until you have something left over.
3. A Light from the Original: God Said "Go", and He Went
Verse 4: "So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him."

Brothers and sisters, there is a very beautiful echo here in the Hebrew. What God said was לֵךְ (*lech*, "go"), and what the text records is וַיֵּלֶךְ אַבְרָם (*vayelech Avram*, "and Abram went"). The same verb. God said "Go", and he went. Not one line of dialogue in between.
He did not ask for an address. He did not ask how long it would take. He did not ask whether there would be a house at the other end. The text records one thing only: he went.

And the second half of verse 4 says, "Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran." Brothers and sisters, seventy-five. At that age most people are thinking about settling down, not about moving house.

Then verse 5 says he took Lot, and their possessions, and their servants, and "they went to go into the land of Canaan" — and the sentence that follows says, "They entered into the land of Canaan." The text walks a very long road in a very short space.

At the end of verse 6 there is a very heavy sentence: "At that time, Canaanites were in the land." Brothers and sisters, God says he is going to give this land to his offspring — and the land is already full of somebody else. Between the promise and the reality stands an entire nation.

Then verse 7: "Yahweh appeared to Abram and said, 'I will give this land to your offspring.' He built an altar there to Yahweh, who had appeared to him." And verse 8 says he pitched his tent again between Bethel and Ai, and "There he built an altar to Yahweh and called on Yahweh's name."

Brothers and sisters, hold on to that pairing: a tent and an altar. A tent can be moved; an altar is fixed to the ground. What he lived in was temporary; the way he worshipped was permanent. If you want to know where a man has really settled, do not look at where he sleeps — look at where he worships. Abraham's house was made of cloth. His altar was made of stone.

And you have heard the phrase "called on Yahweh's name" before — in 4:26, in Seth's line: "At that time men began to call on Yahweh's name." The very same phrase. To call on Yahweh's name on Canaanite ground is to plant a flag. It says who the Lord of this land is.
"So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him" — but he took Lot with him. Does that count as an incomplete obedience?

The text does not rebuke him for taking Lot, but what comes afterwards certainly shows the strain: in chapter 13 the herdsmen of the two households quarrel; in chapter 14 Abram has to go and rescue Lot; in chapter 19 Lot is in Sodom. And the fullest restatement of the promise comes only after Lot has gone (13:14). So the steadier way to put it is this: the text lets us see how an incomplete obedience can still be used by God, and it also lets us see what that incompleteness costs. The reminder for us cuts both ways. On one side, you do not have to stand still because your obedience is not clean enough. On the other, be honest with yourself — some of the things we cannot bear to let go of will send us the bill later on.
4. A Newly Called Man Will Still Reach for His Own Methods
At verse 10 the tone turns without warning: "There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land."

Brothers and sisters, notice what this verse comes straight after. In verse 7 God has only just appeared and said he would give this land to his offspring. In verse 8 he has only just built an altar and called on Yahweh's name. In verse 10 the famine arrives, and down he goes to Egypt.
And the text does not record him asking God about it.
And notice the direction: he went "down" into Egypt. In the geography of Genesis you go up to Canaan and you go down to Egypt. That sense of direction is not merely geographical.

Verses 11 to 13: "When he had come near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, 'See now, I know that you are a beautiful woman to look at. It will happen that when the Egyptians see you, they will say, "This is his wife." They will kill me, but they will save you alive. Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that my soul may live because of you.'"

Brothers and sisters, the text offers not one word in his defence, and it does not add one word of rebuke either. It simply sets down what happened and lets the consequences speak for themselves: Sarai was taken into Pharaoh's house, Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh and his whole household with great plagues, and Pharaoh summoned Abram and said something extremely hard on the ear — "Why didn't you tell me that she was your wife?"
The most embarrassing scene in the whole chapter is this one: a pagan king rebuking the man God chose, for not telling the truth.

But see the other side of it as well: that plague was an intervention, not a revenge. At this point Sarai is the only possible mother of the child of promise. God sent the plague not in order to punish Pharaoh but in order to guard that line. And as it turned out the plague rescued Pharaoh — it let him discover the truth, and he sent Sarai back.
Abram had barely been called before he went down to Egypt and told a lie. How does a man like that end up being called the father of faith?

Because the faith the Bible defines is not perfection; it is "believing God." Romans 4 says, "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness", and that line is quoted out of Genesis 15 — after he had gone down to Egypt and lied. This passage gives us two very important things. First, honesty: the Bible does not prettify its characters, so we do not have to prettify ourselves either. Second, hope: here is a man who stumbled almost as soon as he was called, and God did not swap him out for somebody else. What we have to be careful of is swinging to the other extreme and treating "God will use me anyway" as a permit to do wrong — the outcome of chapter 12 is a whole household escorted out of Egypt, and the cost of it was real.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching the call as though it must mean resigning your job and going into full-time ministry. "Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father's house" was Abram's own specific call on that one occasion; it is not everybody's standard script. Turn it into a rule for everyone and you will leave the brothers and sisters who are faithful in the workplace feeling like second-class Christians. The question actually worth asking is not "do I have to leave?" but "is there something I am gripping that I will not hand over to God?"

The second is preaching "make your name great" as prosperity teaching. In the previous chapter of this very same book, people said, "let's make a name for ourselves", and they were scattered. God makes his name great, and the purpose is written into the same speech — "You will be a blessing", "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you." When the congregation has heard you, what they should be wanting is to be used by God, not to be seen by people.

The third is skipping the trip down to Egypt. Verses 10 to 20 follow immediately upon the great call, and that is the honesty of the Bible. Leave it out and the congregation will assume that people who have been called do not fall — and the next time they themselves fall, they will conclude that they are finished.

The fourth is turning "I will curse him who treats you with contempt" into a talisman for contemporary politics. That sentence is addressed to Abraham and to his offspring, and Galatians 3:16 and 3:29 tell us that the offspring is Christ, and that everyone who belongs to Christ is that offspring. I want to hold both sides here. On one side, antisemitism in any form whatsoever is never to be tolerated — Romans 11 says plainly that God has not rejected his people. On the other side, we do not take the actions of any modern government and equate them directly with the promise of this verse. What the congregation needs is the capacity to discern, not a slogan telling them which side to pick.

The fifth is preaching Abram's descent into Egypt as "how wisely he preserved himself." The consequences in the text have already passed the verdict for us: the household struck with plagues, a rebuke from a pagan king, and an escorted exit with his face in the dust. And what is more serious still, he did the very same thing again later on (chapter 20), and his son Isaac did it too (chapter 26). A weakness that never gets dealt with is handed on to the next generation.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: what Chinese people value most is precisely "your relatives, your father's house" — the falling leaf returning to its root, bringing glory to the ancestors, not travelling far while your parents are alive. God told Abram to leave his father's house. Is that not unfilial? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be said very clearly, or a great many people will be hurt. First, the Bible has never abolished filial duty. The Ten Commandments put "honour your father and mother" first among the commands about people, and 1 Timothy 5:8 says that anyone who does not provide for his own relatives "has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." Second, what Abram left was "the father's house" as a safety net, not "father and mother" as a responsibility. In fact he spent his whole life looking after the people of his family — when his nephew Lot got himself into trouble, Abram marched out overnight to rescue him. Third, the real question here is this: when the expectations of the father's house collide with the call of God, who decides? The Lord Jesus put it very bluntly in Matthew 10:37: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." That is not telling you to love your parents less. It is putting the order straight. And on the pastoral side let me add one thing: a person who genuinely puts God first usually ends up caring for his parents better than before, because what now drives his devotion is no longer guilt. It is love.

The second question: since I came to faith my family have reacted fiercely — some of them say I have turned my back on my ancestors and forgotten where I came from. What am I supposed to do? Brothers and sisters, this is the most real pain a Chinese believer carries. Let me offer three very practical directions. First, do not try to win them with arguments. Abram left behind no manuscript for persuading his father's house of anything; he simply went, and then built an altar in every place he stopped. Your life will speak for you. Second, keep "leaving" and "cutting off" apart. Abram left his father's house, but he never severed the relationship — later on he sent his servant back to his own kindred to find a wife for Isaac. You can walk a different road and still be the dutiful child of that family. Third, remember the purpose: "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you." God chose you not in order to pull you out of your family, but in order to bless that family through you. You may well be the Abraham of your own clan — and that line has to start somewhere. It starts with you.
When a famine comes you find a way through it. Isn't that perfectly normal? Why does the manuscript say he went off course?

There is nothing wrong with finding a way through, and the text never says that going down to Egypt was in itself a sin. What has to be watched is the order. In that whole section there is no record at all of Abram building an altar, or enquiring of God, or praying. He had built an altar at Bethel and called on Yahweh's name — and then the famine came and he simply set off. That is very practical for us: our problem is usually not that we cannot think of a plan; it is that when we think of the plan we step around God on the way. And notice the second move — once he reached Egypt he began telling lies to save his own skin. When the first step taken under pressure is taken without asking God, the second step is very often where the line gives way. So what has to be practised is not "stop looking for solutions." It is "ask one question before you go looking."
7. Living 321 Out — Set Out First, and the Address Follows
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Abram left his father's house; the Lord Jesus left his Father's house. Philippians 2 says he "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." One of them left Ur of the Chaldees; the other left the glory of heaven. Brothers and sisters, this is my role model: for my sake he walked the one road nobody was willing to walk. So when God asks me to put something down, I am not doing anything unprecedented. I am walking in a direction he has already walked.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter gives us a very important standard: the content of a call may be unclear, but the source of a call has to be clear. Abram did not know where he was going, but he knew who was calling him. Brothers and sisters, what most people are anxious about is the first of those; what actually needs settling is the second.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — God said, "go to the land that I will show you", and that showing is in the present continuous. Guidance is not one complete map handed over at the start; it is given to you as you walk. And that is exactly why walking with him matters so much — if the whole map came at once, you would never need to ask him anything tomorrow.

Let Jesus be King — the route map is in his hand, not in mine. To let Jesus be King is to accept that I am given the next step and not the whole journey. Brothers and sisters, this is especially hard for our generation, because we are used to planning: the five-year plan, the retirement projection, the school route mapped out for the children. None of that is sin. But it makes it very easy to forget who is actually doing the arranging.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice that not one line of this promise was won by Abram. The text says nothing whatever about why he was chosen — not one word in praise of his character, his faith or his family line. Joshua 24:2, on the contrary, tells us that his ancestors served other gods. If there is a reason you were chosen, you then have to keep that reason going. If there is no reason at all, the only thing left to you is thanksgiving.

Establish God's system — "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you" is the missionary manifesto of the whole Bible. Brothers and sisters, one man is chosen in order that the blessing may be carried through to all the families. So if you are going to establish God's system, your eyes have to stay on that phrase, "all the families." If the blessing stops with you, then it is not the blessing of this verse.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We often say "change begins with me", and this chapter gives that a very good footnote — God really did begin with one man. But be careful of the other side of it. Abram had not been called long before he went down to Egypt and kept himself alive by his own methods. So "change begins with me" is not the same sentence as "I have already changed." Between being called and being mature there lie several decades. A person may make his decision for Christ today and still handle tomorrow's crisis with his old methods — that is not false faith, that is the real process. In pastoral work, please give people that room. And give yourself that room too.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, the Same Word: "Leave"
Brothers and sisters, that same word — "Leave" — falls into four different hearts and sounds like four completely different things.

The proud heart hears: "I am the Abraham of this generation." This heart very easily treats a call as a promotion in status, and reads "God chose me" as "I must be rather special." Brothers and sisters, notice this: the text is completely silent about why he was chosen, and it remembers his failure with perfect clarity. Being chosen is not a certificate of qualification. It is grace.

The fearful heart hears: "If I do not know where I am going, I dare not move." This heart will pray over one decision for three years, asking and asking again, and still not be certain. To a heart like that I want to say: look at the wording of verse 1. What God gave was not a map. It was a voice. What you have to be certain of is not the route; it is who is speaking. And Psalm 119:105 says his word is "a lamp to my feet" — a lamp lights up what is at your feet, not what is three years down the road.

The ashamed heart hears: "With a background like mine, God probably will not use me." You may feel that you started too late, that your schooling is not enough, that your family is broken, that your past will not bear looking at. Brothers and sisters, Abram was seventy-five, he had no son, and he came out of a family that worshipped idols. And about why God chose him the text does not write a single word — because there was no reason, and that is what grace means. Your background cannot cancel God's call.

The wounded heart hears: "What is he going to take off me this time?" You may have lost a great deal already — a relationship, a job, a child, a dream — and the word "leave" sounds like one more thing about to be taken away. Brothers and sisters, look carefully at where the weight of this call actually falls: of the seven lines, five of them give and only one of them asks. God tells him to leave one thing behind and promises him seven. He has never been the kind who only takes and never gives.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, write down your own "country, relatives, father's house." Which of them is the thing your heart says "I am not safe without it" about? Write it down, and then in prayer hand them over to God one at a time. You do not have to let go straight away. Begin by admitting honestly that it is there.

Second, practise setting out first. Find one thing you already know you ought to do but have been waiting for more certainty about — an apology, an invitation you have never spoken out loud, a piece of service you have never begun — and take the first step this week, without waiting for it all to become clear.
Third, build an altar. Set up one fixed point of worship inside your present circumstances: a time, a place, a stretch of prayer. The house may be rented. The altar has to be stone.

Fourth, pray for somebody from "all the families." Pick a person or a group whose background is completely unlike yours, pray for them this week, and do one concrete thing for them. The blessing God gives you has to have a "for whose sake" on the far end of it.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences: there is a man in the Bible, seventy-five years old, whom God told to leave his homeland without ever telling him where he was going — and he went; the last line of the promise God gave him is "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you" — he was chosen for other people's sake; and yet the very same chapter goes straight on to record that he told a lie to save his own life, and the Bible covers up not one bit of it.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I do not need to know the whole road; I only need to know who it is that is calling me.
I declare that my name is to come from God and not from my own hand; I will no longer go about making a name for myself.
I declare that everything God gives me has a "for whose sake" on the far end of it; the blessing does not stop with me.
I declare that what I live in may be a tent, but my altar is to be made of stone.
This week I am supposed to "leave one thing I have been leaning on" — but I do not know what mine is.

There are three questions that work very well. First: if that thing were taken away tomorrow, what would frighten me most? Your reliance is usually hiding somewhere in the answer. Second: when I make a decision, which item do I count first — money, what other people will think, saving face, or a feeling of security? Third: when pressure comes, what does my hand reach for first — the phone, the fridge, the shopping app, or one particular person? Once you have found it you do not have to give it up all at once. Make one small leaving: one day without touching it, one week without checking it, one occasion where you do not ask that person first. The point of leaving is not asceticism. It is moving your reliance back onto God — and inside that small empty space you will need him, really need him, for the first time.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be a man of seventy-five, leading a camel, walking out through the gate of Haran.
He does not know where he is going. He has no address, no timetable, no guarantee. He has one sentence — one sentence about which he is certain who said it.

Hebrews 11:8-10 sums him up like this: "By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went. By faith he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob … For he was looking for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

Brothers and sisters, notice that last line. The people of the previous chapter threw everything they had into building a city, with a tower whose top reached the sky, and the work stopped. The man of this chapter lives in a tent and builds nothing at all — and Scripture says he was waiting for a city, one "whose builder and maker is God."
The city people built for themselves could never be finished. The city God builds he never once saw in his lifetime — and he waited for it all his life.

And the city he was waiting for is the one we see in Revelation 21: the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. Brothers and sisters, the tower people build goes up; God's city comes down from above. The direction is always the same.

The focus is not on how much I have left behind, not on how far I have travelled, and not on how many times I have fallen along the way. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who left his Father's house, who came down, who died for me, and he is the lamp of that city. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to set out on the strength of one sentence, and to build an altar wherever we come to rest. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of the lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at the level of mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ God's call is "leave" plus "go to the land that I will show you." If you had only the first half of that, what would faith turn into?
2. ★★★ Every strand of the threefold promise points at somebody else by the end of the sentence. How does that correct our understanding of "being blessed"?
3. ★ The original behind "go" is "go for yourself." What good does obedience do to the person himself?
4. ★★ Abram went down to Egypt and told a lie almost as soon as he was called, and the Bible still calls him the father of faith. What does that do to the way you look at your own failures?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can arrange this for myself), fearful (what becomes of me if I leave?), ashamed (I made my resolve and fell the very next moment), wounded (somebody once used the word "obedience" to force me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ "If that thing were taken away tomorrow, what would frighten me most?" Follow that question through, and find the deepest reliance you are living on at present.
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "When pressure comes, the first thing my hand reaches for is …"

9. ★★ This week you are going to make one small leaving where that reliance is concerned — one day without touching it, one week without checking it, one occasion where you do not ask that person first. Say which one you will do.

Leader's reminder: questions nine and ten will touch on addiction and dependency. Do not pass judgement on anybody's reliance in front of the group, and do not require anyone to make the details public. If someone speaks of behaviour that is clearly addictive, follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "You will be a blessing" — inside your own home, who will you give the blessing to this week? Name the person, and name what you are going to do.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: what about at your work or at your school?
12. ★★★ The practice of asking one question first: this week, every time pressure forces a decision on you, stop and ask God one question before you move. Say what you will use to remind yourself.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him what that reliance of yours is, and ask him to check on you on the seventh day. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible, seventy-five years old, who was called to leave his homeland for a place that was never even named. Second, every promise God gave him ends with the same line — "You will be a blessing." Third, so I have begun to believe that the good I have been given is not only for myself. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one small leaving you are going to make this week, and who you are going to tell. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to give us hearts that dare to get up and go — and that are willing to ask him one question first.
